title: Consensus And Information Redistribution In Quantum Networks
authors: J. Novotný, D. Štěrba, I. Jex, H. -H. Kowalski, A. Abedi
abstract: Consensus algorithms are mechanisms driving nodes of a network to agreement. In quantum networks they also redistribute information encoded in the global quantum state, allowing global properties to be inferred from local measurements without reconstructing the global state. Motivated by this, we investigate decentralized quantum consensus in qudit networks governed by discrete random unitary dynamics. We characterize the analytic asymptotic dynamics, identify global information preserved by the evolution, and derive conditions for which different notions of quantum consensus emerge. A general theorem is derived that establishes a unified framework for extracting globally encoded information from local measurements beyond consensus states. First, we analyze CNOT networks and determine which global information can be recovered by individual nodes and which requires joint measurements on cooperating nodes. The CNOT model is well understood and presents a case with entanglement creation - a characteristic quantum feature of networks worth analyzing in detail. Second, we identify the complete class of two-qubit interactions that asymptotically achieve consensus on the average number of excitations, thereby establishing a quantum analogue of classical average consensus. We further show that joint measurements on k cooperating nodes recover exactly the first k moments of the excitation-number distribution.
summary: This work develops a theoretical framework for understanding quantum consensus in networks driven by random unitary dynamics. It shows that global information can be systematically extracted from local measurements by analyzing the moments of the excitation-number distribution. This advances the understanding of information processing in quantum networks beyond simple state reconstruction.
main_problem: The paper investigates how consensus algorithms in quantum networks redistribute global quantum information, allowing global properties to be inferred from local measurements without reconstructing the full global state.
main_result: A general theorem establishes a unified framework for extracting globally encoded information from local measurements, showing that joint measurements on k nodes recover the first k moments of the excitation-number distribution.
method: The analysis uses the attractor formalism applied to discrete random unitary dynamics to characterize the asymptotic behavior of the quantum network.
model_or_system: The system is a qudit network (d-dimensional Hilbert space) whose dynamics are governed by discrete random unitary interactions. Specific models analyzed include CNOT networks and general two-qubit interactions.
key_observables: Quantum consensus states, global information, local measurements, moments of the excitation-number distribution, and the reduced state $ho_i$.
important_parameters: The number of nodes (n), the dimension of the qudits (d), and the specific unitary interaction structure.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the attractor framework for random unitary operations and assumes the dynamics can be modeled by random unitary evolution.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares classical and quantum average consensus, showing the quantum protocol reaches a permutation-symmetric state. Other figures illustrate the network structure and dynamics.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining various forms of quantum consensus (e.g., $\sigma$EC, RSC, SSC), analyzing the asymptotic dynamics using random unitaries, and culminating in a general theorem that links joint local measurements to the recovery of global moments.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical framework for understanding information flow and measurement limitations in complex, interacting quantum systems, which is highly relevant to quantum communication and computation.

The classical protocol iteratively converges to the average of the initial node values, while the quantum protocol uses random unitary op- erations to reach a permutation-symmetric state. Local measurements estimate the average excitation, while collective measurements on m qubits provide access to moments of the excitation-number distribution up to order m.
